PowerScale SDK: Architecture, Security, and API Mapping

This document reviews the Dell PowerScale SDK, including its architecture, security considerations, and a comprehensive mapping of OneFS REST API endpoints to SDK functions, intended for developers and administrators integrating with Dell PowerScale clusters.

    • This SDK simplifies integration with the Platform API (PAPI) and RESTful Access to Namespace (RAN) interfaces, which are core components of the OneFS system.
    • With each SDK package, there should be a guide which will help users to install and use the PowerScale SDK.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) – PowerScale SDK

  • Q. Where can I find the PowerScale SDK documentation?

    The official SDK documentation is available on GitHub https://github.com/Isilon/isilon_sdk  and Dell’s support portal. 

    Q. How do I log a defect?

    Log defects via your internal ticketing system (e.g., Jira, ServiceNow) or Dell Technologies support portal. Include SDK version, OneFS version, API endpoint, request/response payloads, and error messages.

    Q. What details should I include when reporting a defect?

    • - SDK version 
    • OneFS version
    • API endpoint used/ SDK function
    • Response/error
    • Steps to reproduce 
    • Logs or screenshots

    Q. Which Version of python is currently supported

    Python 3.12 ( we also tested with 3.13)

    Q. How is a defect triaged?

    If any issue is logged, then hierarchy should follow as: 

    • First check the modules like ansible which is being written using SDK 
    • Validate if the issue is due to incorrect usage, parameters, or logic in the playbooks (not in our bucket) 
    • If modules are fine, inspect the SDK  
    • Is it parsing responses properly? 
    • Are there any exceptions or misconfigurations? 
    • Check the debug logs or write sample scripts for testing SDK call 
    • If SDK behavior is fine, then inspect API response 
    • Is the API endpoint reachable? 
    • Is the response correct and consistent? 
    • Are there any backend issues on PowerScale? 

    Q. How do I check if an issue is already known?

    Search the GitHub issues page https://github.com/Isilon/isilon_sdk_python/issues, Dell support knowledge base. 

    Q. Can I raise issues publicly?

    Yes, you can raise issues on the GitHub repository as it is open source at https://github.com/Isilon/isilon_sdk_python/issues, for enterprise support, use Dell’s support channels. 

    Q. What if the SDK doesn’t support a specific OneFS version?

    Use the closest compatible SDK version or contact Dell support for guidance. Always match SDK version with OneFS version for best results.

Home > Storage > PowerScale (Isilon) > White Papers > PowerScale SDK: Architecture, Security, and API Mapping > Overview

Overview

  • The PowerScale SDK is a set of tools, documentation, and code samples designed to help developers build applications that interact with Dell PowerScale storage platforms.

    It helps in monitoring and provisioning storage management tasks, managing data access, quotas, snapshots, and replications.

    The PowerScale SDK for Python provides official language bindings for programmatic access to the OneFS API, enabling developers to interact with Dell Technologies Isilon storage clusters using Python.

    This SDK simplifies integration with the Platform API (PAPI) and RESTful Access to Namespace (RAN) interfaces, which are core components of the OneFS system.

    With each SDK package, there should be a guide which will help users to install and use the PowerScale SDK.

    Key Features

    • Language Bindings: Offers Python bindings for OneFS REST APIs, allowing seamless cluster configuration and namespace access.
    • Version-Specific Packages: Supports multiple OneFS versions with dedicated subpackages (e.g., isilon_sdk.v9_12_0 for OneFS 9.12.0).
    • REST API Coverage: Facilitates access to endpoints under https://<cluster>:8080/platform/*, covering a wide range of administrative and data operations.

    Authentication

    The PowerScale SDK interacts with the OneFS Platform API (PAPI), which supports session-based authentication for secure and scalable access to cluster resources. 

    This method is particularly useful for environments requiring temporary access tokens or integration with identity providers. 

    Session Initialization

    A client authenticates using credentials (e.g., username/password) and receives a session token from the OneFS API. 

    Token Usage

    The token is used in subsequent API requests, eliminating the need to send credentials repeatedly. This improves security and performance. 

    Session Expiry

    Tokens are valid for a limited time and expire automatically, reducing the risk of long-term credential exposure. 

    Version Information

    • The PowerScale SDK follows a clear versioning system that matches OneFS releases, making it easier for developers and admins to ensure compatibility
    • Each major SDK release corresponds directly to a OneFSversion like latest is v0.7.0 corresponding to OneFS 9.12
    • And subpackages inside any SDK package will have the following alignments:  

    isilon_sdk.v9_12_0 aligns with OneFS 9.12.0.0  

    isilon_sdk.v9_11_0 aligns with OneFS 9.11.0.0 

    • Now onwards will clearly align SDK versions with OneFS. If OneFS version is 9.13, then SDK version will be v0.13.0
    • First release for OneFS 9.13 -> SDK version v0.13.0 
    • Minor release if any defect fix -> SDK version v0.13.1

    SDK Location

    The PowerScale SDK is available in multiple locations and formats to support flexible deployment and integration with Dell Technologies PowerScale OneFS clusters. 

    Key locations include:

    • PyPI (Python Package Index): Use pip to install the SDK, which includes all supported OneFS subpackages.https://pypi.org/project/isilon-sdk/ 
    • Dell Technologies Community & Documentation: Available through the customer support zone (location TBD).

SDK Security Aspects

Dell.com Contact Us
Share
United States/English

Home > Storage > PowerScale (Isilon) > White Papers > PowerScale SDK: Architecture, Security, and API Mapping > SDK Security Aspects

SDK Security Aspects

    • Security Controls Map: The security controls map shows the network connections and user interfaces for SDK. The map indicates the security controls in SDK that protect the connections and interfaces from attack.

    Figure 1.   Security Controls Map

    • Authentication:  Session-based authentication applies to the sessions created. A JWT token is used to support session-based authentication
    • Authorization:  Authorization controls the permissions and authorized activities of authenticated users and processes
    • Port Usage: The SDK itself does not require or manage specific ports, but since it interacts with OneFS APIs, all necessary API-related ports must be open on the system for proper communication.
    • TLS Support: SDK relies on OneFS API's TLS configuration, supporting standard TLS 1.2 and 1.3 cipher suites for secure communication
    • Data Security: While the SDK itself does not handle encryption, it relies on OneFS APIs, which support TLS for secure communication
    • Hashing: SDK relies on OneFS, which supports secure hashing algorithms like SHA-256
    • Logger: SDK has inbuilt logger module, user can set required log level

Usage

Home > Storage > PowerScale (Isilon) > White Papers > PowerScale SDK: Architecture, Security, and API Mapping > Usage

Usage

  • Installation

    Create a virtual environment before installing the SDK: 

    python3 -m venv sdk_env 
    source sdk_env/bin/activate 

    Install the SDK using Python’s package manager: 

    pip install isilon-sdk 

    Alternatively, clone the GitHub repository for development: 

    git clone https://github.com/Isilon/isilon_sdk_python.git 

    Importing the SDK

    Each OneFS version has its own subpackage. Example for OneFS 9.12: 

    from isilon_sdk.v9_12_0 import Configuration, ApiClient 

    Authentication Setup

    Configure the SDK with cluster credentials: 

    configuration = Configuration() 
    configuration.host = 'https://<cluster_ip>:8080' 
    configuration.username = 'uesrname' 
    configuration.password = 'your_password' 
    configuration.verify_ssl = True 
    api_client = ApiClient(configuration) 

    Making API Calls

    Example: Get cluster configuration 

    from isilon_sdk.v9_12_0 import ClusterApi 
    cluster_api = ClusterApi(api_client) 
    response = cluster_api.get_cluster_config() 

    Common Use Cases

    • Cluster Info: Get system details, version, and status. 
    • Filesystem Access: Manage directories, files, quotas, and snapshots. 
    • Network Config: View or modify SMB/NFS exports. 
    • User Management: Integrate with AD/LDAP, manage roles. 
    • Monitoring: Access performance metrics and health status. 

    Error Handling

    Use try-except blocks to catch API errors: 

    from isilon_sdk.v9_12_0.rest import ApiException 
    try: 
         response = cluster_api.get_cluster_config() 
    except ApiException as e: 
         print(f"API error: {e}") 

    Logging and Debugging

    Enable debug logging: 

    import logging 
    logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG) 

    Version Compatibility

    • OneFS 9.12 → isilon_sdk.v9_12_0 
    • OneFS 9.11 → isilon_sdk.v9_11_0

Home > Storage > PowerScale (Isilon) > White Papers > PowerScale SDK: Architecture, Security, and API Mapping > User prerequisites for security updates

User prerequisites for security updates

    • Prerequisites: Before applying the latest SDK package, ensure all required conditions are met. Select the appropriate sub-package from the PowerScale SDK based on the OneFS version available to the user
    • Authencity and Integrity: Dell Technologies will sign the SDK package. To verify that an installation package remains unaltered after downloading.
    • Applicable Release: Use signed releases from trusted sources (e.g., GitHub or PyPI)
    • Hash Verification: Validate the downloaded package using published SHA-256 hashes

    GPG Signature Verification (if available):

    Import the maintainer’s public GPG key:

    gpg --import <Public Key Filename>

    Verify the signature:

    gpg --verify <signature filename> <tar.gz filename>

    If the signature is valid, you will see something like this: 

                     gpg: Signature made <Timestamp> 
                                                       gpg:  using RSA key <RSA Key>                  

    gpg: Good signature from "Dell Technologies Inc. < support@dell.com >"
